questions.stem: A whiteboard, which is \(1.2\text{ m}\) wide, is to be placed in the exact centre of a classroom wall. The total length of the wall from left to right is \(6\text{ m}\). What is the distance from the left-hand edge of the wall to the left-hand edge of the whiteboard?
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Convert all measurements to the same unit (metres):
Wall length \(= 6\text{ m}\)
Whiteboard width \(= 1.2\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Find the total leftover space on the wall by subtracting the whiteboard width from the total wall length:
\(\text{Leftover space} = 6\text{ m} - 1.2\text{ m} = 4.8\text{ m}\).

Step 3: Since the whiteboard is centered, this leftover space is divided equally between the left and right sides:
\(\text{Left side distance} = \frac{4.8\text{ m}}{2} = 2.4\text{ m}\).

questions.stem: Three different packets of nuts were purchased. Packet A contained \(650\text{ g}\), Packet B contained \(1.4\text{ kg}\), and Packet C contained \(850\text{ g}\). If these are mixed together in one large container, what is the total mass of the mixture, in both kilograms and grams?
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Convert all masses to grams to add them easily:
Packet A \(= 650\text{ g}\)
Packet B \(= 1.4 \times 1000 = 1400\text{ g}\)
Packet C \(= 850\text{ g}\)

Step 2: Add the weights together:
\(\text{Total Mass} = 650 + 1400 + 850 = 2900\text{ g}\)

Step 3: Convert the total back to kilograms:
\(2900 \div 1000 = 2.9\text{ kg}\)

Therefore, the total mass is \(2.9\text{ kg}\) or \(2900\text{ g}\).

questions.stem: Markers on a running track are placed \(50\text{ m}\) apart. If the total distance from the first marker to the last one is \(2\text{ km}\), how many markers are there in total?
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Convert the total track distance to metres:
\(2\text{ km} = 2000\text{ m}\).

Step 2: Calculate the number of intervals between the markers:
\(\text{Intervals} = \frac{2000\text{ m}}{50\text{ m}} = 40\).

Step 3: Since there is a marker at both the starting and ending point, the number of markers is always \(1\) more than the number of intervals:
\(\text{Total markers} = 40 + 1 = 41\).

questions.stem:
Aled has the following items in his school bag. Knowing that \(1\text{ mL}\) of water has a mass of \(1\text{ g}\), and the empty school bag itself weighs \(1.5\text{ kg}\), what is the total mass of Aled’s bag and its contents?
  • Laptop computer (\(2.8\text{ kg}\))
  • Sandwich (\(180\text{ g}\))
  • Water bottle (\(20\text{ g}\) empty bottle, filled with \(450\text{ mL}\) of water)
  • Orange (\(85\text{ g}\))
  • School books (\(760\text{ g}\))
  • Pencil case (\(387\text{ g}\))
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: List and convert all individual items to grams (\(1\text{ kg} = 1000\text{ g}\)):

  • Empty bag \(= 1.5\text{ kg} = 1500\text{ g}\)

  • Sandwich \(= 180\text{ g}\)

  • School books \(= 760\text{ g}\)

\(\text{Total Mass} = 1500 + 2800 + 180 + 470 + 85 + 760 + 387 = 6182\text{ g}\)

Step 3: Convert to kilograms:
\(6182 \div 1000 = 6.182\text{ kg}\)

questions.stem: Convert \(53\text{ cm}^2\) to \(\text{m}^2\).

steps.explain: Since \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\), a square metre is \(100 \times 100 = 10\,000\text{ cm}^2\). To convert cm² to m², divide by 10,000.
Pitfall: using the LINEAR factor (÷100) instead of squaring it (÷10,000) gives \(0.53\) (option B) — area conversions always use the SQUARED factor.

meta.sourcePaper: Hornsby Girls HS — Year 7 Assessment 3, Term 4 2024

questions.stem: Convert \(0.14\text{ ha}\) to \(\text{m}^2\).

steps.explain: 1 hectare = 10,000 m². Multiply by 10,000 to convert hectares to m².
Pitfall: using the wrong power of 10 (×1000 instead of ×10,000) gives \(140\) (option B); (×100,000) gives \(14\,000\) (option C).

meta.sourcePaper: Hornsby Girls HS — Year 7 Assessment 3, Term 4 2024

questions.stem: Convert \(47\,258\text{ cm}^3\) to \(\text{m}^3\).

steps.explain: Since \(1\text{ m}=100\text{ cm}\), a cubic metre is \(100^3 = 1\,000\,000\text{ cm}^3\). To convert cm³ to m³, divide by 1,000,000.
Pitfall: using the SQUARED factor (÷10,000, as for area) instead of the CUBED factor (÷1,000,000) gives \(4.7258\) (option B) — volume conversions always cube the linear factor.

meta.sourcePaper: Hornsby Girls HS — Year 7 Assessment 3, Term 4 2024

questions.stem: Convert \(0.035\text{ L}\) to \(\text{cm}^3\).

steps.explain: \(1\text{ L} = 1000\text{ cm}^3\). Multiply by 1000.
Pitfall: using ×100 instead of ×1000 gives \(3.5\) (option B); using ×10,000 gives \(350\) (option C).

questions.stem: Which is the best value: \(6\) oranges for \(\$2.52\) or \(45\) oranges for \(\$18.45\)?
options: Both offer exactly the same value
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Calculate the unit cost of the first option (6 oranges):
\(\text{Unit cost} = \frac{\$2.52}{6} = \$0.42\text{ per orange}\)

Step 2: Calculate the unit cost of the second option (45 oranges):
\(\text{Unit cost} = \frac{\$18.45}{45} = \$0.41\text{ per orange}\)

Step 3: Compare the two unit costs. Since \(\$0.41 < \$0.42\), buying 45 oranges is the cheaper, better value option.

questions.stem: If a generator needs \(24\text{ L}\) of fuel to run for \(4\) days, for how long can it run on \(90\text{ L}\) of fuel?
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Find the rate of fuel consumption per day:
\(\text{Fuel per day} = \frac{24\text{ L}}{4\text{ days}} = 6\text{ L/day}\)

Step 2: Divide the total fuel available (\(90\text{ L}\)) by the daily consumption rate (\(6\text{ L/day}\)):
\(\text{Days} = \frac{90\text{ L}}{6\text{ L/day}} = 15\text{ days}\)

questions.stem: A staircase-shaped figure (not to scale, all angles are right angles) has an overall top width of \(7.23\text{ mm}\), a right-most height of \(8.16\text{ mm}\), and one visible step segment of \(4.02\text{ mm}\). Find the perimeter, correct to 1 decimal place.
questions.hint: For any rectilinear "staircase" shape (only right angles, no diagonal cuts), the total of all rightward horizontal steps equals the overall top width, and the total of all downward vertical steps equals the overall right-hand height.

steps.explain: For a staircase shape made only of right angles, every horizontal "step in" is matched by an equal "step out" further along, so the TOTAL horizontal distance across all the steps (shown in blue) equals the overall top-to-bottom bounding width, \(7.23\text{ mm}\) — counted TWICE, once for the top set of steps and once along the bottom.

figure.svg: fig:7145ef82c9

steps.explain: Likewise, the TOTAL vertical distance down all the steps (shown in orange, on the right) equals the overall left-to-right bounding height, \(8.16\text{ mm}\) — also counted TWICE, once down the right-hand steps and once up the left side.

figure.svg: fig:5ec5ee7c9b

steps.explain: Pitfall: simply adding the three given numbers together (\(7.23+4.02+8.16=19.41\), option B) ignores that every notch has a matching return segment — always use the general "2×(width+height)" rule for staircase shapes instead of guessing which numbers to add.

figure.svg: fig:32840beb5c

questions.stem: Two sides of a triangle measure 6 cm and 12 cm. Which one of these statements about the length of the third side is true?
options: Its length is greater than 6 cm but less than 18 cm.
Its length is less than 6 cm.
Its length is greater than 18 cm.
questions.hint: For any triangle, the third side is greater than the difference of the other two sides and less than their sum.

steps.explain: For the third side x, the triangle inequality says x must exceed the difference of the other sides.
It must also be smaller than the sum of the two known sides.
Combine the strict inequalities; endpoints would make a straight, degenerate triangle.
Choose the statement expressing this interval.

questions.stem: Goran made a triangle using string. The perimeter of Goran's triangle was 16 cm. Which of these could be the side lengths of his triangle?
questions.hint: Check that the three lengths add to 16 cm and that the sum of any two sides is greater than the third.

steps.explain: The three sides must add to the given perimeter of 16 cm.
The option 5, 5, 6 totals 16.
Check triangle feasibility: the sum of any two sides must exceed the third. Here 5+5>6, 5+6>5, and 5+6>5.
Therefore these lengths form a possible triangle.

questions.stem: Sabre wants to frame a square photograph that has an area of 64 square centimetres. Sabre makes the frame using 4 strips of aluminium. Each strip is 4 centimetres longer than the width of the photograph. What is the total length of the 4 strips aluminium he uses to make the frame?
questions.hint: Find the photograph’s side from its area, then add 4 cm for each of the four strips.

steps.explain: The photo is square with area 64 cm², so its side s satisfies s²=64.
Each of the four aluminium strips is 4 cm longer than one photo side.
Add four equal strips.
State the total aluminium length.

questions.stem: Aragorn is fencing a paddock on his property. The total length of fencing he requires is 8.2 kilometres. The length of the paddock is 2.8 kilometres. How wide is the paddock? Write your answer, in kilometres to one decimal place?
questions.hint: Use P=2L+2W and isolate W.

steps.explain: Use the rectangle perimeter formula with length 2.8 km and total fencing 8.2 km.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 150" width="360" height="104" role="img" aria-label="Step 1: highlighted Use the rectangle perimeter formula with length 2.8 km and total fencing 8.2 km."><rect x="2" y="2" width="516" height="146" rx="16" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#dbe4f0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="18" y="18" width="8" height="112" rx="4" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="42" y="46" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Step 1</text><text x="42" y="78" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#475569">Use the rectangle perimeter formula with len</text><text x="42" y="116" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e1b4b">2L+2W=8.2</text><rect x="424" y="48" width="78" height="64" rx="2" fill="#eaf2ff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M424 112H502" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="6"/><text x="463" y="133" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#334155">highlighted part</text></svg>

steps.explain: Substitute L and subtract its two sides.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 150" width="360" height="104" role="img" aria-label="Step 2: highlighted Substitute L and subtract its two sides."><rect x="2" y="2" width="516" height="146" rx="16" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#dbe4f0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="18" y="18" width="8" height="112" rx="4" fill="#0284c7"/><text x="42" y="46" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Step 2</text><text x="42" y="78" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#475569">Substitute L and subtract its two sides.</text><text x="42" y="116" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e1b4b">2W=8.2-2(2.8)=8.2-5.6=2.6</text><rect x="424" y="48" width="78" height="64" rx="2" fill="#eaf2ff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M424 112H502" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="6"/><text x="463" y="133" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#334155">highlighted part</text></svg>

questions.stem: Ronald places 5 identical hexagonal tiles side-by-side to make the pattern pictured below. Each tile has a perimeter of 24 cm and is in the shape of a regular hexagon. What is the perimeter of the large shape, in centimetres?
questions.hint: Each hexagon side is one-sixth of its perimeter. Count the exposed edges in the 5-tile arrangement.

steps.explain: Each regular hexagon has six equal edges and perimeter 24 cm.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 150" width="360" height="104" role="img" aria-label="Step 1: highlighted Each regular hexagon has six equal edges and perimeter 24 cm."><rect x="2" y="2" width="516" height="146" rx="16" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#dbe4f0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="18" y="18" width="8" height="112" rx="4" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="42" y="46" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Step 1</text><text x="42" y="78" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#475569">Each regular hexagon has six equal edges and</text><text x="42" y="116" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e1b4b">24÷6=4 cm per edge</text><path d="M438 50L470 50L488 78L470 106L438 106L420 78Z" fill="#f3e8ff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M438 50L470 50L488 78" fill="none" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="6"/><text x="454" y="127" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#334155">outside edge</text></svg>

steps.explain: The row pattern has 16 exposed hexagon edges; shared edges are excluded.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 150" width="360" height="104" role="img" aria-label="Step 2: highlighted The row pattern has 16 exposed hexagon edges; shared edges are excluded."><rect x="2" y="2" width="516" height="146" rx="16" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#dbe4f0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="18" y="18" width="8" height="112" rx="4" fill="#0284c7"/><text x="42" y="46" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Step 2</text><text x="42" y="78" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#475569">The row pattern has 16 exposed hexagon edges</text><text x="42" y="116" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e1b4b">Exposed edges=16</text><path d="M438 50L470 50L488 78L470 106L438 106L420 78Z" fill="#f3e8ff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M438 50L470 50L488 78" fill="none" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="6"/><text x="454" y="127" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#334155">outside edge</text></svg>

questions.stem: A square has an area of 169 square centimetres. What is the perimeter?
questions.hint: Find the square side using the square root of its area, then multiply by four.

steps.explain: A square’s area is side × side. Let the side length be s.
Take the positive square root because a length cannot be negative.
A square has four equal sides.
State the perimeter.

questions.stem: Anthony creates a tile pattern using tiles in the shape of regular hexagons. The perimeter of each tile is 24 cm. He keeps adding tiles in the same way until he has a row with a perimeter of 120 cm. How many tiles are in Anthony’s row?
questions.hint: Each new hexagon shares one full side with the row. Find the length of one side, then subtract the shared edge from the outside perimeter.

steps.explain: A regular hexagon has six equal sides. Divide its perimeter equally among those sides to find the length marked in blue.

steps.explain: Each grid square is 1 square unit. For each triangle, count its base and perpendicular height in grid-square lengths.

questions.stem: Bob had a mini tennis court in his backyard, as shown in the diagram below. What is the area of the mini tennis court?
questions.hint: Use area = length × width and read both dimensions from the court diagram.

steps.explain: The mini court is the inner rectangle on the grid. Count 6 squares across and 4 squares down; the legend says each square is 1 m².

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 150" width="360" height="104" role="img" aria-label="Step 1: highlighted Read the mini court’s length and width from the plan."><rect x="2" y="2" width="516" height="146" rx="16" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#dbe4f0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="18" y="18" width="8" height="112" rx="4" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="42" y="46" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Step 1</text><text x="42" y="78" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#475569">Read the mini court’s length and width from </text><text x="42" y="116" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e1b4b">l=6 m, w=4 m</text><rect x="424" y="48" width="78" height="64" rx="2" fill="#eaf2ff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M424 112H502" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="6"/><text x="463" y="133" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#334155">highlighted part</text></svg>

steps.explain: For a rectangle, area is the number of unit squares in each row multiplied by the number of rows.

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 150" width="360" height="104" role="img" aria-label="Step 2: highlighted A rectangle’s area is length times width."><rect x="2" y="2" width="516" height="146" rx="16" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#dbe4f0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="18" y="18" width="8" height="112" rx="4" fill="#0284c7"/><text x="42" y="46" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Step 2</text><text x="42" y="78" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#475569">A rectangle’s area is length times width.</text><text x="42" y="116" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e1b4b">A=lw</text><rect x="424" y="48" width="78" height="64" rx="2" fill="#eaf2ff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M424 112H502" stroke="#0284c7" stroke-width="6"/><text x="463" y="133" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#334155">highlighted part</text></svg>

steps.explain: Multiply the grid dimensions.

questions.stem: Find the area of the following composite shape.
questions.hint: Split the shape into two rectangles. Find the missing side lengths first.

steps.explain: The shape can be split into two rectangles.
Missing right vertical side \(y = 9 - 5 = 4 \text{ cm}\).
Missing top horizontal side \(x = 12 - 4 = 8 \text{ cm}\) (assuming the bottom right extension is 4 cm wide based on tick marks in original, or derived from splitting).
Wait, the solution says \(y = 9 - 5 = 4\) cm and \(x = 12 - 4 = 8\) cm.
Let's assume the indent width is equal to \(y\), making the bottom right piece a \(4 \times 4\) square.
Area 1 (left rectangle) = \( 9 \times 8 = 72 \text{ cm}^2 \).
Area 2 (right square) = \( 4 \times 4 = 16 \text{ cm}^2 \).
Total Area = \( 72 + 16 = 88 \text{ cm}^2 \).

questions.stem: Find the area of the following composite shape.
questions.hint: Subtract the area of the triangle from the area of the square.

steps.explain: Area of the square = \( 9 \times 9 = 81 \text{ cm}^2 \)
The missing piece is a triangle with base = \( 4 + 5 = 9 \text{ cm}\) (wait, looking at the solution: \( \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 4 \)).
Ah, the base of the triangle cut out is 5 cm, and the height is 4 cm.
Area of the triangle = \( \frac{1}{2} \times 5 \times 4 = 10 \text{ cm}^2 \)
Total Area = \( 81 - 10 = 71 \text{ cm}^2 \).

questions.stem: Here is a plan of Dave's backyard. The total area of the paving stones is 18 m². What is the total area of the grass in Dave's backyard?
questions.hint: Use the paving-stone grid to find the area represented by one square, then count the grass squares.

steps.explain: The plan shows grass and paving as a 3:1 area ratio; paving represents one equal part and totals 18 m².

figure.svg: <svg xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" viewBox="0 0 520 150" width="360" height="104" role="img" aria-label="Step 1: highlighted The plan shows grass and paving as a 3:1 area ratio; paving represents one equal part and totals 18 m²."><rect x="2" y="2" width="516" height="146" rx="16" fill="#f8fafc" stroke="#dbe4f0" stroke-width="2"/><rect x="18" y="18" width="8" height="112" rx="4" fill="#7c3aed"/><text x="42" y="46" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="19" font-weight="700" fill="#334155">Step 1</text><text x="42" y="78" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="15" fill="#475569">The plan shows grass and paving as a 3:1 are</text><text x="42" y="116" font-family="Arial,sans-serif" font-size="18" font-weight="700" fill="#1e1b4b">1 part=18 m²</text><rect x="424" y="48" width="78" height="64" rx="2" fill="#eaf2ff" stroke="#475569" stroke-width="3"/><path d="M424 112H502" stroke="#7c3aed" stroke-width="6"/><text x="463" y="133" text-anchor="middle" font-family="Arial" font-size="13" fill="#334155">highlighted part</text></svg>

steps.explain: Grass covers three equal parts.

questions.hint: Find the combined triangle’s base and perpendicular height from the two square side lengths.

steps.explain: The two square areas are 25 cm² and 4 cm², so their side lengths are 5 cm and 2 cm.

questions.stem: Find the area of a parallelogram (not to scale) with base \(7\text{ cm}\) and perpendicular height \(5\text{ cm}\).

steps.explain: The area of a parallelogram is base × perpendicular height — unlike a triangle, there is NO factor of \(\dfrac{1}{2}\). The perpendicular height is the dashed line meeting the base at a right angle, not the slanted side.

questions.hint: Use half × base × perpendicular height; the diagram shows a 7 m base and 4 m height.

steps.explain: The diagram gives a triangle base of 7 m and perpendicular height 4 m; the courtyard dimensions are context only.

questions.stem: This triangle was made by cutting a square in half. The perimeter of the triangle is 51.21 cm. What is the area of the triangle?
questions.hint: Use the labelled 21.21 cm diagonal as one side of the perimeter. The other two sides are equal because the triangle is half of a square.

steps.explain: Cutting a square along its diagonal makes two congruent right-isosceles triangles. The given 21.21 cm is the diagonal side; the two legs are equal. Let each leg be s.

steps.explain: The perimeter is the sum of all three sides. Substitute the two equal legs and the labelled diagonal, then isolate s.

steps.explain: The two legs meet at the right angle, so they can be used as the perpendicular base and height. Both are 15 cm.

questions.stem: Ky designs an outdoor table that is in the shape of a trapezium. The dimensions of the table top are shown in the picture below. What is the area of Ky’s table top?
questions.hint: For a trapezium, area is half the sum of the parallel sides times the perpendicular height.

steps.explain: Identify the parallel sides of the trapezium as 50 cm and 80 cm, with perpendicular height 40 cm.

steps.explain: Use half the sum of the parallel sides times the height.

questions.stem: Florence used identical cubes to build a rectangular prism. There were 16 cubes in its base. She used 80 cubes altogether. Which of these could be the dimensions of Florence’s prism?
questions.hint: The base dimensions must multiply to 16 and all three dimensions must multiply to 80.

steps.explain: The base contains 16 identical cubes, so length×width must equal 16.
Divide the total cube count by the base count to find the height.
Choose base factors 2 and 8, which multiply to 16, with height 5.
State a possible set of dimensions.

questions.stem: Two identical solid cubes are placed at the bottom of a fish tank. The fish tank is then completely filled, as shown below. What is the volume of the water that surrounds the cubes? Give your answer in cubic centimetres.
questions.hint: Find the tank volume, then subtract the volume of both solid cubes.

steps.explain: Read the tank dimensions 80 cm by 40 cm by 60 cm and compute the full prism volume.

questions.stem: A small shipping container is the shape of a rectangular prism. The volume of the small shipping container is 6 cubic metres. A large shipping container has dimensions that are double the dimensions of the small shipping container. What is the volume of the large shipping container?
questions.hint: Doubling each of three dimensions multiplies volume by 2³.

steps.explain: The large container doubles the length, width and height of the small one.
Volume scales by the product of all three dimension scale factors.
Multiply the original volume by 8.
State the large container volume.

It is solid brick but has a hole that goes from one side to the other which is 3 bricks high and two bricks wide, as shown in the diagram. How many bricks are in the stack?
questions.hint: Subtract the through-hole volume from the full rectangular prism of bricks.

questions.stem: What is the time \(4\text{ hours, } 22\text{ minutes}\) after \(10:45\text{ a.m.}\)?
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Start at \(10:45\text{ a.m.}\).

Step 2: Add \(4\text{ hours}\):
\(10:45\text{ a.m.} + 4\text{ hours} = 2:45\text{ p.m.}\) (since we pass 12:00 p.m. noon).

Step 3: Add \(22\text{ minutes}\) to \(2:45\text{ p.m.}\).
\(45 + 22 = 67\text{ minutes} = 1\text{ hour and } 7\text{ minutes}\).
\(2:45\text{ p.m.} + 1\text{ hour } 7\text{ minutes} = 3:07\text{ p.m.}\).

questions.stem: Calculate the time elapsed between \(8\text{ p.m.}\) on Monday and \(7:35\text{ a.m.}\) on Wednesday.
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Count the time from Monday 8 p.m. to Tuesday 8 p.m.:
This is exactly \(24\text{ hours}\).

Step 2: Count the time from Tuesday 8 p.m. to Wednesday 8 a.m. (the next morning):
This is exactly \(12\text{ hours}\).
Accumulated total \(= 24 + 12 = 36\text{ hours}\) (representing Wednesday 8:00 a.m.).

Step 3: Since the end time is 7:35 a.m., which is \(25\text{ minutes}\) before 8:00 a.m., we subtract \(25\text{ minutes}\) from \(36\text{ hours}\):
\(36\text{ hours} - 25\text{ minutes} = 35\text{ hours and } 35\text{ minutes}\).

questions.stem: Calculate the difference between two finish times for a race: \(02:28:15\) and \(03:42:38\).
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Subtract the earlier finish time (\(02:28:15\)) from the later finish time (\(03:42:38\)):

\(\begin{aligned} \text{Hours difference:} & \quad 3 - 2 = 1\text{ hour} \\ \text{Minutes difference:} & \quad 42 - 28 = 14\text{ minutes} \\ \text{Seconds difference:} & \quad 38 - 15 = 23\text{ seconds} \end{aligned}\)

Therefore, the time difference is \(1\text{ hour, } 14\text{ minutes, and } 23\text{ seconds}\).

questions.stem: What is the time \(4\text{ hours, } 18\text{ minutes and } 45\text{ seconds}\) after \(3:15\text{ p.m.}\)?
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Start with the initial time: \(3\text{ p.m.} \; 15\text{ minutes} \; 00\text{ seconds}\).

Step 2: Add the hours:
\(3\text{ p.m.} + 4\text{ hours} = 7\text{ p.m.}\)

Step 3: Add the minutes:
\(15\text{ minutes} + 18\text{ minutes} = 33\text{ minutes}\)

Step 4: Add the seconds:
\(00\text{ seconds} + 45\text{ seconds} = 45\text{ seconds}\)

The resulting time is \(7:33:45\text{ p.m.}\).

questions.stem: Calculate the time elapsed between \(9:15\text{ a.m.}\) and \(4:12\text{ p.m.}\) on the same day.
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Step 1: Convert both times to 24-hour format:
\(9:15\text{ a.m.} \rightarrow 09:15\)
\(4:12\text{ p.m.} \rightarrow 16:12\)

Step 2: Subtract the start time from the end time:
\(16:12 - 09:15\)

Since 12 minutes is less than 15 minutes, borrow 1 hour (60 minutes) from 16:
\(16:12 = 15:72\)
\(15:72 - 09:15 = 6\text{ hours and } 57\text{ minutes}\).

questions.stem: What is the day and time \(3\text{ days, } 14\text{ hours and } 8\text{ minutes}\) before midnight on Friday?
questions.solution:
Step-by-step breakdown:

Midnight on Friday is equivalent to Friday 12:00 a.m. (or the very start of Saturday).

Step 1: Go back exactly \(3\) days from Friday midnight:
This brings us to Tuesday midnight (12:00 a.m.).

Step 2: Go back \(14\text{ hours}\) from Tuesday midnight:
Going back \(12\text{ hours}\) brings us to Monday noon (12:00 p.m.).
Going back another \(2\text{ hours}\) brings us to Monday 10:00 a.m..

Step 3: Go back \(8\text{ minutes}\) from Monday 10:00 a.m.:
\(10:00\text{ a.m.} - 8\text{ minutes} =\) Monday 9:52 a.m..
